questions.stem: „Seit drei Jahren gibt es in unserer Stadt ein Repair-Café. Jeden ersten Samstag im Monat reparieren Freiwillige kostenlos Toaster, Fahrräder und Kleidung. Ziel ist es, weniger wegzuwerfen.“ What is the main aim of the Repair-Café?
options: To train young people as paid repair technicians
To collect broken goods for recycling each month
To throw away less by repairing things for free
To sell second-hand toasters and bicycles cheaply
questions.explanation: „Ziel ist es, weniger wegzuwerfen“ states the aim directly, and „Freiwillige reparieren kostenlos“ says how. Nothing is sold, and the volunteers are not paid.

questions.stem: „Immer mehr Städte richten Fahrradstraßen ein, auf denen Autos nur Gäste sind. Radfahrer dürfen dort nebeneinander fahren, und Autos müssen sich anpassen.“ According to the text, what is a Fahrradstraße?
options: A street where cyclists have priority and cars must adapt
A street where bicycles are banned during the daytime
A separate cycle path built alongside a motorway or highway
A street set aside for shops that sell bicycles
questions.explanation: Cars are „nur Gäste“ (only guests) and „müssen sich anpassen“ (must adapt), so cyclists come first. Cars are still allowed, which rules out a separate path.

questions.stem: „Sicher, Hausaufgaben können nerven. Trotzdem halte ich sie für sinnvoll, weil man den Stoff nur durch Üben wirklich behält.“ What is the writer's position?
options: For homework, but only on weekends and in the holidays
For homework, because practice helps you retain what you learn
Against homework, because it annoys students too much
Against homework, because practice in class is more than enough
questions.explanation: „Sicher …“ concedes the opposing point, and „trotzdem halte ich sie für sinnvoll“ gives the writer's actual view, with „weil“ supplying the reason. Stopping at the concession reverses the position.

questions.stem: „Der Roman beginnt langsam, fast zäh. Wer aber durchhält, wird mit einem überraschenden Ende belohnt.“ What is the reviewer's judgement?
options: Fast-paced from the start, but the ending is a disappointment
Slow throughout, so most readers give up before the end
Surprising at the very start, but slow and tough going towards the end
Slow at first, but the surprising ending rewards readers who persist
questions.explanation: „Zäh“ means heavy going, and „wer aber durchhält“ (but whoever perseveres) turns to the reward. The structure moves from criticism to praise.

questions.stem: „Viele Menschen wohnen gern auf dem Land. Allerdings fehlt es dort oft an Ärzten und Busverbindungen.“ What does „Allerdings“ introduce?
options: A repetition of the first statement in other words
A drawback that qualifies the first statement
An example that supports the first statement
A conclusion drawn from the first statement
questions.explanation: „Allerdings“ (however, admittedly) limits what has just been said. Spotting such connectives is how a reader follows the line of an argument.

questions.stem: „Zusammenfassend lässt sich sagen, dass die Vorteile die Nachteile überwiegen.“ What is this sentence doing?
options: Giving one example of a particular advantage
Asking the reader to weigh up both sides of the argument alone
Concluding that the advantages outweigh the disadvantages
Introducing the disadvantages for the first time
questions.explanation: „Zusammenfassend“ (in summary) signals a conclusion, and „überwiegen“ means to outweigh. This is how an evaluative text typically ends.

questions.stem: „Die Bibliothek bleibt vom 20. Dezember bis zum 6. Januar geschlossen. Bücher können in dieser Zeit in den Rückgabekasten am Eingang geworfen werden.“ What can borrowers do while the library is closed?
options: Borrow books from the box at the entrance
Renew their books online until 6 January
Collect their reserved books on 20 December
Return books through the box at the entrance
questions.explanation: „Der Rückgabekasten“ is a returns box: „die Rückgabe“ means return. The text says nothing about borrowing or renewing during the closure.

questions.stem: „Kinder unter sechs Jahren nur in Begleitung eines Erwachsenen.“ What does the notice mean?
options: Adults may only enter with a child under six
Children under six must be accompanied by an adult
Children under six are not allowed in at all
Children over six must be accompanied by an adult
questions.explanation: „In Begleitung“ means accompanied, and „unter sechs Jahren“ is under six. Notices often drop the verb, so the meaning comes from the phrases.

questions.stem: „Teilnehmen können alle Schülerinnen und Schüler zwischen 15 und 19 Jahren. Die Texte dürfen höchstens 500 Wörter lang sein und müssen bis zum 30. April eingereicht werden.“ Which entry would be accepted?
options: A 400-word text by an 18-year-old, sent on 5 May
A 450-word text by a 17-year-old, sent on 20 April
A 600-word text by a 16-year-old, sent on 1 April
A 300-word text by a 14-year-old, sent on 10 April
questions.explanation: Only one entry meets all three conditions: age 15–19, „höchstens“ (at most) 500 words, and in by 30 April. Each of the others fails exactly one condition.

questions.stem: „Die Familie Weber wanderte 1952 nach Australien aus. Der Vater fand zunächst Arbeit beim Bau des Snowy-Mountains-Wasserkraftwerks, später eröffnete er eine Bäckerei in Adelaide.“ What did the father do first?
options: Opened a bakery of his own in Adelaide
Worked as a baker in the Snowy Mountains
Built houses for other newly arrived migrants in Adelaide
Worked on building the Snowy Mountains hydro scheme
questions.explanation: „Zunächst“ (at first) marks the hydro scheme as his first job, and „später“ (later) marks the bakery. Many European migrants worked on the scheme after the Second World War.

questions.stem: „Wegen des Streiks fielen gestern zahlreiche Flüge aus.“ What happened?
options: Most flights left on time despite the strike
Many flights were completely full because of the strike
Many flights were cancelled because of the strike
Many flights were delayed because of the storm
questions.explanation: „Der Streik“ is a strike, not „der Sturm“ (storm), and „ausfallen“ means to be cancelled. „Zahlreich“ means numerous.

questions.stem: „Haustiere sind in der Wohnung nicht erlaubt; Ausnahmen gelten nur für Kleintiere wie Fische oder Hamster.“ Which pet may a tenant keep?
options: A pony
A hamster
A dog
A cat
questions.explanation: Pets are banned with an exception for „Kleintiere“ (small animals) such as fish and hamsters. „Ausnahmen gelten nur für“ means exceptions apply only to.

questions.stem: „Bitte füllen Sie das Formular in Druckbuchstaben aus und legen Sie eine Kopie Ihres Reisepasses bei.“ What must you do?
options: Complete the form in block letters and enclose a passport copy
Print out the form and bring your original passport to the office
Fill in the form online and upload a recent photo
Sign the form and post your original passport
questions.explanation: „Druckbuchstaben“ are block capitals, and „beilegen“ is to enclose. The text asks for „eine Kopie“, so the original passport stays with you.

questions.stem: „Die Zahl der Auszubildenden ist im Vergleich zum Vorjahr um fünf Prozent gesunken.“ What does the sentence report?
options: The number of trainees rose by five per cent on the year before
The number of trainees fell to five per cent of all workers
The number of trainees stayed at five per cent of all workers
The number of trainees fell by five per cent on the year before
questions.explanation: „Gesunken“ is the participle of „sinken“ (to fall), and „um“ gives the size of the change. „Auf fünf Prozent“ would give the new level instead.

questions.stem: „Laut Polizei wurde bei dem Unfall niemand verletzt.“ What does the report say?
options: The police were injured while attending the accident
The police have not yet said whether anyone at all was hurt
According to the police, nobody was injured in the accident
According to the police, several people were injured
questions.explanation: „Laut Polizei“ means according to the police, and „niemand wurde verletzt“ is a passive: nobody was injured.

questions.stem: „Hat jemand Tipps für eine günstige Unterkunft in Zürich? Ich bin Student und kann höchstens 40 Franken pro Nacht ausgeben.“ What is the writer looking for?
options: A student job in Zurich paying 40 francs an hour
A room in Zurich to share with 40 other students
Travel tips for a 40-day trip by train around Switzerland
Cheap accommodation in Zurich for at most 40 francs a night
questions.explanation: „Die Unterkunft“ is accommodation and „günstig“ is cheap. „Höchstens 40 Franken pro Nacht“ sets the limit; Switzerland uses the franc.

questions.stem: „Das Konzert war restlos ausverkauft; selbst Stehplätze waren nicht mehr zu bekommen.“ What does „restlos ausverkauft“ mean?
options: Cancelled at the last minute
Completely sold out
Sold out except for standing room
Sold at a reduced price
questions.explanation: „Restlos“ means without remainder, and the second clause confirms it: not even standing places („Stehplätze“) were left.

questions.stem: „Der Bürgermeister hat angekündigt, das Freibad trotz der hohen Kosten zu erhalten.“ What has the mayor announced?
options: The council has received the outdoor pool as a gift
A new indoor pool will be built to replace it
The outdoor pool will be kept open despite the high costs
The outdoor pool will close because of the high costs
questions.explanation: „Erhalten“ can mean to receive, but with „trotz der hohen Kosten“ it means to preserve or keep. Context decides between the two meanings.

questions.stem: „Die Firma hat im letzten Jahr dreißig neue Stellen geschaffen.“ What does the sentence say?
options: The company managed to fill thirty positions last year
The company moved to thirty new sites last year
The company cut thirty jobs last year
The company created thirty new jobs last year
questions.explanation: „Geschaffen“ is from strong „schaffen“ (to create), while weak „schaffen“ (geschafft) means to manage. „Die Stelle“ here is a job, not a place.

questions.stem: „Mit dreißig bekam meine Freundin Torschlusspanik: Plötzlich wollte sie heiraten, ein Haus kaufen und eine Weltreise machen – alles auf einmal.“ What is „Torschlusspanik“?
options: Anxiety about travelling long distances alone
Nervousness in the days before a big exam or interview
Panic that time to reach life goals is running out
Fear of being locked out of one's own house
questions.explanation: Literally panic at the gate closing, the word has no English equivalent. The rush of plans after „mit dreißig“ shows the sense of time running out.

questions.stem: „Natürlich ist es bequem, alles online zu bestellen. Aber wer denkt dabei an die Verkäuferin im Laden um die Ecke, die bald vielleicht keinen Job mehr hat?“ What is the writer's attitude to online shopping?
options: Worried: online orders are often wrongly delivered
Critical: convenience comes at a cost to local shop staff
Enthusiastic: it saves time and creates new jobs
Neutral: it has no real effect on local businesses either way
questions.explanation: „Natürlich ist es bequem“ concedes the benefit, and the rhetorical question after „aber“ turns it into criticism. The concern is local jobs, not delivery errors.

questions.stem: „Super, die neue Umgehungsstraße ist endlich fertig – nach nur zwölf Jahren Bauzeit.“ What is the writer's tone?
options: Angry that the new road has been cancelled
Ironic about how long the road took to build
Proud of how quickly the road was built
Neutral, simply reporting that the road is open
questions.explanation: „Nur zwölf Jahren“ pairs 'only' with a very long time, and „endlich“ (at last) adds to it. The praise in „Super“ is therefore ironic.

questions.stem: „Ehrlich gesagt hatte ich vor meinem Austausch in Hamburg Angst, dass ich niemanden verstehen würde. Nach zwei Wochen träumte ich schon auf Deutsch!“ How did the writer's feelings change?
options: From confidence in German to worry about the exchange family
From enjoying Hamburg to wanting to go back home
From fear of not understanding to feeling at home in German
From excitement about the exchange to disappointment
questions.explanation: „Angst, dass ich niemanden verstehen würde“ is the starting worry, and dreaming in German after two weeks shows it disappeared. „Schon“ stresses how quickly.

questions.stem: „Ob ein Tempolimit auf der Autobahn sinnvoll ist, darüber wird seit Jahren gestritten. Befürworter verweisen auf weniger Unfälle und Emissionen, Gegner auf die persönliche Freiheit.“ What does the writer do?
options: Argue strongly in favour of a speed limit
Argue strongly against a speed limit
Report that a speed limit has been introduced
Present both sides without taking a position
questions.explanation: „Befürworter“ (supporters) and „Gegner“ (opponents) are each given their argument, and the writer adds no judgement. This is informative writing, not persuasive.

questions.stem: „Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren, hiermit möchte ich mich über den Zustand des Zimmers beschweren, das ich vom 3. bis 7. Juli in Ihrem Hotel gebucht hatte.“ What kind of text is this?
options: A personal diary entry about a holiday
An advertisement for a hotel room
A friendly email booking a room
A formal letter of complaint to a hotel
questions.explanation: „Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren“ is a formal opening, and „sich beschweren über“ is to complain about. „Hiermit“ (hereby) is typical of formal letters.

questions.stem: „Liebes Tagebuch, heute war einer der schlimmsten Tage meines Lebens.“ What text type does this open?
options: A journal entry
A formal report
A news article
A product review
questions.explanation: „Das Tagebuch“ is a diary or journal, and addressing it directly is a common way to begin a personal journal entry.

questions.stem: „Es könnte sein, dass die Mieten weiter steigen, sicher ist das aber nicht.“ How certain is the writer?
options: Completely certain that rents will keep rising
Certain that rents will soon fall
Unsure whether rents have risen before
Unsure: a rise is possible but not certain
questions.explanation: „Es könnte sein“ (it could be) uses Konjunktiv II to hedge, and „sicher ist das aber nicht“ states the doubt outright. Hedging language signals a cautious, informative stance.

questions.stem: „Du willst die Welt verändern? Dann fang bei dir an! Komm zu unserem Infoabend am Donnerstag und erfahre, wie du dich in deiner Gemeinde engagieren kannst.“ What is the purpose of the text?
options: To invite young people to an information evening on volunteering
To report on a volunteering event that was held last Thursday
To criticise young people for not doing volunteer work
To advertise paid jobs with the local council
questions.explanation: The imperatives „fang an“ and „komm“ invite the reader to act, and „Infoabend am Donnerstag“ names the event. „Sich engagieren“ means to get involved, unpaid.

questions.stem: „Liebe Kolleginnen und Kollegen, wir möchten Sie herzlich zu unserer Weihnachtsfeier am 15. Dezember einladen.“ Which features mark this as a polite invitation to colleagues?
options: Technical terms and statistics about the company
A friendly group greeting with the polite form „Sie“
The informal „du“ together with slang expressions
Short notes, abbreviations and missing verbs throughout
questions.explanation: „Liebe Kolleginnen und Kollegen“ greets the group warmly, while „Sie“ keeps the respectful distance usual at work. Recognising register is part of reading for audience and purpose.

questions.stem: „Also: Lasst das Auto stehen und steigt aufs Rad – eure Gesundheit und die Umwelt werden es euch danken!“ What is the writer doing?
options: Reporting on the health of cyclists
Urging readers to cycle instead of driving
Advising readers to buy a new car
Thanking readers for cycling to work
questions.explanation: The „ihr“ imperatives „lasst“ and „steigt“ give a call to action, and the promise of thanks from health and environment is the persuasive payoff.

questions.stem: „Die Sportmedizinerin Dr. Lehmann betont: Kinder brauchen Bewegung, und zwei Stunden Sport pro Woche reichen nicht aus.“ Why does the writer include this?
options: To advertise Dr Lehmann's new sports medicine practice
To prove that two hours of sport is enough
To support the argument with an expert's authority
To show that experts disagree about sport
questions.explanation: Citing a sports doctor lends expert weight to the claim. She says two hours „reichen nicht aus“ (are not enough), so the text does not say two hours is enough.

questions.stem: „Betreten der Baustelle verboten! Eltern haften für ihre Kinder.“ What does the sign say?
options: Children may enter the building site with their parents
Keep off the building site; parents are liable for their children
The building site is open to families with children
Parents must keep their children away from the playground nearby
questions.explanation: „Das Betreten … verboten“ forbids entry, and „haften für“ means to be legally responsible for. „Die Baustelle“ is a building site.

questions.stem: „Als ich nach zehn Jahren in mein Dorf zurückkehrte, gab es den Bäcker nicht mehr, und die Schule war ein Wohnhaus geworden. Nur die Kirche stand noch, wie immer.“ What impression does the writer give?
options: Nothing at all in the village has changed in ten years
The writer is pleased that the old school has closed
The village has changed greatly, with little still the same
The village has grown, with many new shops, houses and schools
questions.explanation: The bakery is gone and the school is now a house; „nur die Kirche“ is the one exception. „Nur“ and „wie immer“ throw the changes into relief.

questions.stem: „Ich bin in Wien aufgewachsen, lebe aber seit zwanzig Jahren in Melbourne. Wenn ich heute Wien besuche, fühle ich mich manchmal wie eine Touristin in meiner eigenen Stadt.“ What does the writer suggest?
options: She has never felt truly at home in Vienna, even as a child
She prefers being a tourist to living anywhere
Melbourne reminds her of Vienna every day
Long absence has made her home city feel partly foreign
questions.explanation: „Wie eine Touristin in meiner eigenen Stadt“ captures the paradox of being both insider and outsider. „Seit zwanzig Jahren“ explains why.

questions.stem: „Mein Bruder hat sein Studium nach zwei Semestern abgebrochen. Meine Eltern haben nichts gesagt, aber beim Abendessen war es sehr still.“ What does the writer imply?
options: Nobody in the family noticed the change
The brother had finished his degree early
The parents disapproved without saying so
The parents openly praised the decision
questions.explanation: „Nichts gesagt, aber … sehr still“ shows disapproval through silence rather than words. „Abgebrochen“ means he dropped out, so he did not finish.

questions.stem: „Meine Gastmutter fragte jeden Morgen, ob ich gut geschlafen hätte, und stellte mir immer ein Glas frisch gepressten Orangensaft hin.“ What impression of the host mother does this give?
options: Expecting the writer to cook
Caring and attentive
Strict and distant
Too busy to notice the writer
questions.explanation: Asking every morning and always preparing fresh juice show care. „Jeden Morgen“ and „immer“ make it a habit, not a one-off.

questions.stem: „Wer in Deutschland zu einer Party eingeladen wird, bringt oft eine Kleinigkeit mit – Blumen, Wein oder Pralinen. Mit leeren Händen zu kommen, gilt als unhöflich.“ What does the text suggest?
options: Bringing a gift is considered impolite
Guests are expected to bring a small gift
Guests should bring an expensive present
Hosts give small gifts to their guests
questions.explanation: „Eine Kleinigkeit“ is a small thing, and arriving „mit leeren Händen“ (empty-handed) „gilt als unhöflich“, is considered rude. The gift is small, not expensive.

questions.stem: Text A: „Ein Smartphone gehört nicht in die Hände von Zehnjährigen.“ Text B: „Mit klaren Regeln kann ein Smartphone auch Kindern nützen.“ How do the views differ?
options: A asks for clear rules for children; B asks for a complete ban
Both say phones are useful only for older people
A rejects phones for ten-year-olds; B accepts them with rules
Both reject phones for children whatever the rules
questions.explanation: „Gehört nicht in die Hände von“ is a firm no, while „mit klaren Regeln … nützen“ is a conditional yes. Comparing perspectives like this is a key Unit 4 skill.

questions.stem: Text A (an advert): „Unser Hotel – Ruhe pur, direkt am See!“ Text B (a guest review): „Schöne Lage, aber nachts laute Musik von der Bar.“ What does Text B add?
options: It confirms that the hotel is quiet at night
It says the hotel is a long way from the lake and the beach
It praises the music played at the hotel bar
It challenges the advert's promise of peace and quiet
questions.explanation: The review agrees about the location („schöne Lage“) but „laute Musik“ contradicts „Ruhe pur“ (pure peace). Setting an advert against a review exposes the gap.

questions.stem: Oma: „Früher haben wir Briefe geschrieben und wochenlang auf Antwort gewartet.“ Enkelin: „Heute bin ich genervt, wenn nach fünf Minuten keine Antwort kommt.“ What contrast emerges?
options: Both of them prefer writing letters to sending messages
The granddaughter writes longer messages than her grandmother
The grandmother still waits weeks for her messages today
Expectations about how fast a reply comes have changed hugely
questions.explanation: „Wochenlang“ (for weeks) and „nach fünf Minuten“ mark the two ends of the contrast. „Früher … heute“ frames it as a change over time.
